title: Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Dancings, Damascus
description: New Testament chronology dates its documents; this article tests one of them as an ancestor. It proposes a literary-genealogical test for the priority question: a literature proposed as earliest should exhibit recoverable ancestry, its load-bearing forms derivable from independently attested antecedents, while the forms that follow it may show transformations of it. On that test the received sequence is anomalous: it begins with the literature whose immediate Christian ancestry must be reconstructed, as the field's own category 'pre-Pauline' concedes, and ends with the literature whose ancestry can be read. The article separates three claims collapsed under 'Revelation First' (absolute, corpus and generative priority), audits the chronological gate (the Nero cipher, and the Gallio synchronism, whose one material anchor dates the proconsul and names no letter), and reports two executed results: Revelation 1–3 is the earliest extant Christian text constructed as a closed seven-church corpus, and a machine census of some seventy thousand units of the relevant Greek finds στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς unique to Rev. 2.10 and Jas 1.12, with the common-source audit run and defeat conditions stated. A directional microtest finds the ordered triad work, toil, endurance in exactly two of some 69,400 units, Rev. 2.2 and 1 Thess. 1.3. Revelation First is distinct from the early dating of Revelation: a pre-70 date is not yet priority. It becomes a falsifiable research programme with its first arrows drawn. Version 8 (10 November 2026, in place) adds the commission: each proclamation is addressed to a messenger and the seer is commanded to write and send, set out as an arrow toward the letters to churches with its direction open; and records Philo's lampstand as an extant antecedent for the figure in the midst of the seven (#1758). Version 9 (11 November 2026, in place) traces the figure in the midst to Zechariah's vision of Ἰησοῦς the high priest, robed in the ποδήρης and twice given the name Ἀνατολή, which Philo takes for the Logos while withholding its addressee, and sets the Philonic organization of the scene as its antecedent against the richer alternatives (#1758 v1.1); it draws a second arrow, not yet run, to Hebrews 4.8–14, which gathers the two Joshuas, the two-edged word and the great high priest named Jesus.

methodology: The ancestry test classes the antecedents of each load-bearing feature as extant, independently attested, reconstructed, or unexplained. Lexical markedness is established by machine census over seated, commit-pinned Greek corpora (Septuagint, New Testament, Apostolic Fathers, Philo, Josephus, and the Greek pseudepigrapha, with the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs in Charles's edition): about seventy thousand units for στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς and 69,397 units for the work–toil–endurance triad. The common-source audit is run against the best candidate comparanda (among them T. Job 4.4–11 and Philo, Migr. 133), and the chronological gate is audited link by link.
falsification_conditions: Section VIII states the conditions under which each level fails. Absolute priority fails if the Nero solution fixes composition after 54 CE and the Gallio correlation of 1 Thessalonians stands. Corpus priority fails if a sevenfold Pauline collection is shown before Revelation. The crown-of-life arrow is reopened by a pre-Revelation attestation of στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς, or by a common source that explains both texts better than dependence.

wiki_article: Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles is an article by Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, published in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics and deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 3 November 2026. It proposes a literary-genealogical test for the order of the New Testament's documents: a literature proposed as earliest should show recoverable ancestry, while later forms show transformations of it. On that test the received sequence is anomalous, since the Pauline letters require a reconstructed 'pre-Pauline' layer while Revelation's images announce their antecedents in the prophetic scriptures. The article separates absolute, corpus and generative priority, audits the chronological gate set by the Nero cipher and the Gallio inscription, and reports two executed results: Revelation 1–3 as the earliest extant closed seven-church corpus, read by the Muratorian Fragment as the order Paul followed, and a machine census finding the phrase 'crown of life' (στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς) only in Revelation 2.10 and James 1.12. It distinguishes Revelation First from the older argument for an early date of Revelation and states the conditions under which each claim would fail. Version 8 (10 November 2026) adds the commission, the address of each proclamation to a messenger and the command to write and send, as an arrow toward the letters to churches whose direction is left open, and records the figure in the midst of the seven lampstands, with Zechariah's and Philo's lampstand, as an ancestry case, drawing on In the Midst of the Seven (#1758). Version 9 (11 November 2026) adds, from the second version of In the Midst of the Seven, Zechariah's vision of Joshua the high priest and Philo's organization of the lampstand as antecedents of the figure in the midst, and an arrow toward Hebrews 4.8–14, left unrun.

defines_concepts.definition: In Revelation First: Literary Genealogy, the test that a literature proposed as earliest exhibit recoverable ancestry, each load-bearing feature classed as having an extant antecedent, an independently attested tradition, a reconstructed antecedent, or none.

In Revelation First: Literary Genealogy, the claim that Revelation's sevenfold address to churches preceded and helped generate the construal of Paul's letters as a closed corpus to seven churches, whether or not individual letters were older.

In Revelation First: Literary Genealogy, the claim that particular structures compressed in Revelation were elaborated by later texts, whether or not Revelation preceded every one of them in absolute date.
